newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. says rains may slow Rwanda refugee airlift.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says rains may slow Rwanda refugee airlift.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency said it was aiming to start a massive airlift of Rwandans from camps in Zaire on Friday but heavy rains and bad roads might slow the operation.

"We are still hoping to get the first plane off on Friday but it is pouring down now following heavy rains overnight," said UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg on Thursday in the northeastern Zairean capital of Kisangani.
"We have enough trucks to pick up the refugees south of Kisangani for each flight but with these rains the roads will become very difficult. They will become a quagmire," he added.
The U.N. airlift of an estimated 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees south of rebel-held Kisangani will be one of the biggest such operations and will cost millions of dollars.

Asked about the regional governor's concern that an epidemic of cholera among the Hutu refugees might spread to the Zairean population if the airlift began, Stromberg said: "We are confident we can bring out people who don't have cholera."
He said the number of deaths from cholera among the refugees had risen to 19 among 303 cases but 42 of the sick were released on Wednesday after receiving medical treatment in the camps.
The first group of Rwandan refugees due to be flown out on Friday from Kisangani to the eastern city of Goma before being trucked back to Rwanda consists of 80 unaccompanied children.

An estimated 50,000 refugees are camped out at Kasese, 29 km (17 miles) south of Kisangani, with a similar number in makeshift camps further south after months of trekking west to escape rebels until the northeast capital fell in mid-March.
Stromberg said the U.N. had two Ilyushin-76s and a Hercules C-130 for the airlift and might bring in another Ilyushin. The three Ilyushins could carry 1,500 refugees on two flights to Goma each day.
"The air capacity is basically in place and we're bringing in fuel," he said. "But the state of the road for trucks to take them to the airport in Kisangani each day will be a problem."
The refugees are the rump of more than two million Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 after the victory of Tutsi rebels in the civil war and the genocide of 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
Most returned home late last year but about 300,000 are believed to be stranded in Zaire, with the largest concentration between Kisangani and Ubundu, 125 km (75 miles) to the south.

Rebel chief Laurent Kabila came under international pressure this month to agree to the airlift after earlier insisting the refugees should be trucked home, though the roads are impassable for long stretches.

The refugees are in a very poor state after trekking about 600 km (375 miles) since last October through dense jungle where they survived on grubs and tree-bark. They marched westwards to flee Tutsi-dominated rebels, supported by Rwanda's government.
U.N. officials said the Rwandan government refused to allow the planes with refugees fly direct to the capital Kigali, arguing it would cause congestion at the city's main airport.
Stromberg said a train which returned from Ubundu to Kisangani on Wednesday brought back 389 refugees including 58 refugees who emerged from the forest after 44 others had died.
